taxonomy.title: Trauma — head, spine, pelvis and extremities
taxonomy.scopeIn: Head injury, GCS, spinal injury, traumatic cerebrovascular injury, pelvic ring stabilization, limb trauma and compartment/vascular assessment.
taxonomy.scopeOut: Nontraumatic nerve localization belongs to neuro-orthopedic-essentials. Pelvic visceral injury and global survey belong to trauma-initial-abdomen. Generic reversal biology belongs to hematology-transfusion-coagulation.

researchAgenda: Pelvic hemorrhage and extremity compartment priorities

secondaryBoundaryEntries.title: Trauma — initial assessment and abdominal injury

secondaryBoundaryEntries.priorityReason: A central trauma lane appears largely absent from the existing live objectives.

secondaryBoundaryEntries.scopeOut: Pediatric testis/hydrocele belongs to pediatric-neck-thoracic-gu. Pelvic trauma stabilization belongs to trauma-head-spine-extremities. Primary appendicitis belongs to appendix-appendicitis.

assignment.ownerDirection: I feel like they are still a little confusing and we may be missing some of the concepts that are most tested and testable. ... look up everything they can about that topic and decide what concepts on that are the most testable. Then look at all the questions that fit in that topic category and critically analyze if it is a good question based on the rules and feedback you have gotten from me on what is a good and what is a bad question. Then the worker also looks for gaps on that topic that it can fill in with more questions. Remember to try to create multiple part questions when possible. ... The goal of this is to increase the number of questions, fill gaps, test the testable stuff, and to make the current existing questions better and more accurate. Also remember that the questions need to be difficult.

question.stem: Which verbal/motor entry and reassessment plan should be recorded for {patientName}'s second examination?
question.explanation: Do not trend a manufactured total across an untestable verbal component. Equally, do not attribute every apparent change to the tube: the motor examination has changed from following commands to normal flexion/withdrawal. Record the observed components, mark verbal testing NT with its interference, and communicate the motor change for prompt reassessment. These observations do not by themselves select a CT or neurosurgical operation.

question.stem: Which next assessment best addresses {patientName}'s later examination despite an unchanged best-motor GCS entry?
question.explanation: GCS uses the best motor response, but that summary must not erase a newly different response on the other side. The right arm still follows commands while the left now withdraws, under an unchanged sedative exposure. Urgent cranial imaging is the best offered next assessment of the new focal change. Keep the component observations and the intubation-related verbal limitation visible. The exact trauma imaging priority is source-held for verification; no sedative-clearance interval or diagnostic imaging finding is invented.

exhibit.caption: Constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations
cells: Withdraws from nail-bed pressure but does not lift two fingers on request
Glucose 116 mg/dL; arterial CO2 43 mmHg; sedative infusion unchanged

answerChoices.label: Urgent noncontrast cranial computed tomography
answerChoices.rationale: A new unilateral loss of command following is not captured by recording the best arm response; it needs urgent structural neurologic reassessment.

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced brain magnetic resonance imaging
answerChoices.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging can clarify selected neurologic findings, but noncontrast CT is the appropriate first structural study for this new acute traumatic change.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Magnetic resonance imaging can clarify selected neurologic findings, but noncontrast CT is the appropriate first structural study for this new acute traumatic change.

answerChoices.label: Repeat arterial blood-gas sampling with carbon-dioxide review
answerChoices.rationale: Gas exchange is important but the near-stable measurements and lateralized motor pattern do not make a generalized carbon-dioxide effect the leading unresolved issue.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Gas exchange is important but the near-stable measurements and lateralized motor pattern do not make a generalized carbon-dioxide effect the leading unresolved issue.

nodes.displayName: Escalate a new focal motor change despite an unchanged best GCS response
nodes.learningObjective: Escalate a new focal motor change despite an unchanged best GCS response
nodes.task: Which assessment plan should Daniel's team choose after the second motor examination?
nodes.currentUpdate: Daniel is intubated after the crash. Circulation is stable, and there is no ongoing extracranial hemorrhage.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record. Fictional observations.

items.label: Motor record
items.value: First assessment: both arms show two fingers on request. Second assessment: the right still shows two fingers, while the left withdraws from pressure and does not follow the request. A second examiner reproduces the change.

items.label: GCS chart
items.value: The best motor entry is M6 at both assessments. The tube prevents verbal testing.

items.label: Treatment and limb record
items.value: The sedative infusion is unchanged and there was no intervening bolus. The left arm has no fracture or local injury.

choices.label: Noncontrast head CT now
choices.rationale: The best motor entry still reflects the right arm, but it conceals a confirmed new left-sided change. That pattern under unchanged sedation warrants acute structural brain reassessment.
choices.temptation: Reconciles the summary score with the limb-specific observations.
choices.counterfactual: A confirmed new unilateral change remains an indication to reassess structural injury.

choices.label: Reduce sedation and repeat the motor examination
choices.rationale: A wake-up examination can clarify drug-related impairment. The new unilateral change is confirmed under unchanged exposure while the other arm still follows commands, so using medication adjustment as the next assessment can delay structural reassessment.
choices.temptation: Attributes the apparent change to intubation or drug interference because the best response remains recorded as M6.
choices.counterfactual: New bilateral depression after a sedative increase, with no focal asymmetry, would strengthen medication-related reassessment.

choices.label: Brain MRI without contrast now
choices.rationale: MRI can characterize selected injuries that CT underdetects. The acute question is whether a structural change requires prompt neurosurgical management, making noncontrast CT the first offered study.
choices.temptation: Selects a detailed modality for unexplained weakness.
choices.counterfactual: Persisting deficits after acute CT-based assessment can justify MRI.

nodes.explanation: The best motor entry still reflects the right arm, but it conceals a confirmed new left-sided change. That pattern under unchanged sedation warrants acute structural brain reassessment.
nodes.identityDecision: Preserve the stable concept. This is a new question version with the same clinical meaning.
reasoningSteps: Reconcile an unchanged best motor entry with a confirmed loss of command following in the opposite arm.
Use the lateralized pattern and drug-exposure chronology to choose structural reassessment over a medication wake-up test.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Interpreting the unchanged M6 summary as evidence that the new asymmetry can be deferred to a sedation reassessment.
nodes.decidingObservation: The left arm changes while the right retains command following under the same sedative exposure.
nodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If both arms became less responsive after an increased infusion and there were no focal change, reducing sedation and repeating the examination would become the credible offered assessment.
nodes.deletionTest: The chart's repeated M6 entry creates the actual competing interpretation. The limb observations overturn it. Exposure chronology distinguishes a medication-related change. Removing the serial findings removes the reason to prioritize CT.

authorGate.coverTheKey: Removed the completed gas and normal CO2 row. CT and MRI now share the same urgency wording. The medication plan tests the actual global-score error, and the stem asks about a change rather than an examination. The later CT remains concealed.
authorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: Three assessment plans for the immediate reassessment of the recorded motor change.
twoConsequentialSteps: Reconcile an unchanged best motor entry with a confirmed loss of command following in the opposite arm.
Use the lateralized pattern and drug-exposure chronology to choose structural reassessment over a medication wake-up test.
authorGate.residentDifficulty: Fair moderate. The competing sedation assessment is credible when the learner relies on the unchanged best-response entry. No hard-difficulty claim is made.
authorGate.oneDefensibleKey: The confirmed asymmetry under unchanged exposure supports CT among the offered plans. Existing focal-change source/editorial holds remain carried.
authorGate.disposition: One revision completed. New exact version requires independent reassessment and remains needs_clinician_review.

nodes.displayName: Apply acute subdural evacuation criteria despite preserved responsiveness
nodes.learningObjective: Apply acute subdural evacuation criteria despite preserved responsiveness
nodes.task: Which neurosurgical plan best fits Daniel's newly returned CT and examination?
nodes.currentUpdate: During the later assessment Daniel still opens his eyes to sound and follows commands with his right arm.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record. Fictional observations.

items.label: CT report
items.value: Acute right convexity subdural blood measures 12 mm in maximum thickness, with 3 mm midline shift.

items.label: Current examination
items.value: Left arm remains weaker. Pupils are reactive. No active extracranial bleeding is recorded.

choices.label: Urgent operative hematoma evacuation
choices.rationale: The 12 mm acute subdural collection exceeds the guideline thickness criterion. Preserved command following and modest shift do not remove the indication for urgent neurosurgical evacuation.
choices.temptation: Applies the lesion measurement despite a partly reassuring examination.
choices.counterfactual: A surgically significant acute hematoma keeps evacuation appropriate.

choices.label: Neurosurgical observation with serial CT
choices.rationale: Observation can fit a small, stable collection without operative features. Its use here overlooks the independently significant thickness.
choices.temptation: Overweights the modest midline shift and preserved command following.
choices.counterfactual: A smaller stable collection with no deterioration or other operative indication could support observation.

choices.label: Intracranial-pressure monitoring with medical treatment
choices.rationale: Monitoring can guide care for selected severe injury without a surgical mass lesion. It does not address the evacuable collection.
choices.temptation: Treats monitoring as the next step before deciding on evacuation.
choices.counterfactual: Coma with concern for intracranial hypertension and no surgical mass lesion could favor monitoring.

nodes.explanation: The 12 mm acute subdural collection exceeds the guideline thickness criterion. Preserved command following and modest shift do not remove the indication for urgent neurosurgical evacuation.
nodes.identityDecision: New scored objective and new concept identity.
reasoningSteps: Interpret both thickness and shift, recognizing that either criterion can determine intervention.
Choose evacuation despite preserved responsiveness rather than substitute surveillance or monitoring.
nodes.closestCredibleError: the modest shift can distract from a separate operative thickness criterion
nodes.decidingObservation: The acute collection is 12 mm thick.
nodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If the collection measured 4 mm with minimal shift and the examination were stable without focal loss, observation would become the reasonable offered plan.
nodes.deletionTest: The measured thickness and concurrent examination earn the treatment decision. Removing the CT leaves no lesion-specific basis for choosing evacuation.

authorGate.coverTheKey: Covered the key, no diagnosis in the complaint supplies an action. Three management plans are specific. The preceding CT explanation omits size cutoffs and does not name this later plan.
authorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: Every option answers the same task at the stated care-planning stage. Specific parallel actions were compared in full context.
twoConsequentialSteps: Interpret both thickness and shift, recognizing that either criterion can determine intervention.
Choose evacuation despite preserved responsiveness rather than substitute surveillance or monitoring.
authorGate.residentDifficulty: Predicted moderate or hard for PGY-2/3 because the modest shift can distract from a separate operative thickness criterion
authorGate.oneDefensibleKey: The acute collection is 12 mm thick. Counterfactual re-solve. If the collection measured 4 mm with minimal shift and the examination were stable without focal loss, observation would become the reasonable offered plan.
authorGate.disposition: Author self-check completed. Independent adversarial review and exact clinical review remain pending.

nodes.displayName: Choose disposition after a negative CT in a baseline anticoagulated adult
nodes.learningObjective: Choose disposition after a negative CT in a baseline anticoagulated adult
nodes.task: Which head-injury disposition best fits Lena's completed hospital assessment?
nodes.currentUpdate: The head CT shows no hemorrhage. Routine wound care, delayed-hemorrhage precautions and follow-up instructions are common to the proposed plans.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record. Fictional observations.

items.label: First interview
items.value: During an English-language interview Lena gave no intelligible answers to orientation questions. The triage note recorded a verbal-response concern.

items.label: Subsequent assessment
items.value: With a qualified interpreter, Lena correctly states her name, the hospital, the date and the fall sequence. Limb movements are symmetric. Her partner confirms that her speech and behavior match the usual baseline.

items.label: Course and support
items.value: Headache has improved, she walks with her usual gait and drinks without vomiting. Her partner will remain with her and can obtain emergency help.

items.label: Medication record
items.value: Apixaban was taken on the injury day.

choices.label: Home care after the completed assessment
choices.rationale: The interpreted assessment resolves the apparent verbal concern and establishes Lena's baseline status. With a negative CT and suitable supervision, anticoagulant exposure by itself does not require routine admission or another scan.
choices.temptation: Uses the reliability of the later examination before applying the negative-CT disposition boundary.
choices.counterfactual: A new deficit, persistent unexplained confusion or unsuitable support would change the discharge assessment.

choices.label: Hospital observation with serial examinations
choices.rationale: Observation can fit an unresolved neurologic abnormality or another admission need. The initial communication problem has been resolved by a reliable examination rather than simply ignored.
choices.temptation: Carries the first verbal concern forward as a persistent clinical abnormality.
choices.counterfactual: Persistent abnormal behavior through a reliable interpreter would favor continued hospital assessment.

choices.label: Hospital observation with scheduled repeat CT
choices.rationale: Routine repeat imaging is tempting during apixaban use. It is not supported solely by that exposure after the represented negative CT and baseline reassessment.
choices.temptation: Applies the initial-imaging concern to an automatic second scan.
choices.counterfactual: New neurologic deterioration would justify a new acute imaging decision.

nodes.explanation: The interpreted assessment resolves the apparent verbal concern and establishes Lena's baseline status. With a negative CT and suitable supervision, anticoagulant exposure by itself does not require routine admission or another scan.
nodes.identityDecision: New meaning requires a new concept identity. Prior histories remain on the previous concepts.
reasoningSteps: Distinguish a communication-limited first interview from a reliable later neurologic assessment at baseline.
Apply the completed negative CT and actual home support to head-injury disposition.
nodes.closestCredibleError: Treating the first verbal-response concern as ongoing impairment or treating apixaban as an automatic repeat-scan admission indication.
nodes.decidingObservation: Orientation and baseline behavior are established through reliable communication, with suitable supervision after a negative CT.
nodes.decisionChangingCounterfactual: If the interpreter-assisted examination remained confused or the partner described new abnormal behavior, home care would lose its basis and hospital reassessment would be appropriate.
nodes.deletionTest: The first and later interviews make evidence reliability consequential. Removing either leaves the source of the verbal concern unresolved. Supervision and current clinical course determine whether discharge is supportable.

authorGate.coverTheKey: Removed 'discharge-stage', the irrelevant additional-antithrombotic sentence, the global no-admission-indication conclusion and the MRI foil. Safety instructions are common context and the three options are parallel disposition strategies.
authorGate.decisionStageAndCategory: Three head-injury disposition plans after completed CT and reassessment.
twoConsequentialSteps: Distinguish a communication-limited first interview from a reliable later neurologic assessment at baseline.
Apply the completed negative CT and actual home support to head-injury disposition.
authorGate.residentDifficulty: Fair moderate. A resident must resolve the discordant verbal record before applying the anticoagulant disposition rule.
authorGate.oneDefensibleKey: The reliable baseline examination, negative CT and supervision support home care among these options. The historical owner decision hold remains open.
authorGate.disposition: One revision completed. New exact version requires independent reassessment and remains needs_clinician_review.

nodes.displayName: Correct ineffective pelvic compression using its anatomic position
nodes.learningObjective: Correct ineffective pelvic compression using its anatomic position
nodes.task: Which binder adjustment best fits Nora's recorded placement?
nodes.currentUpdate: Nora has a pelvic ring disruption with blood-component resuscitation underway. The team checks the temporary binder before further transport.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record. Fictional observations.

items.label: Device position
items.value: The center of the binder lies across the iliac crests, above the palpable greater trochanters.

choices.label: Move the binder center to the greater trochanters
choices.rationale: The recorded binder is too high for the intended pelvic compression position. Centering at the greater trochanters corrects the documented placement problem; this is a technique fact rather than a difficult source-and-treatment decision.
choices.temptation: Attention may go to device tension rather than its anatomical level.
choices.counterfactual: If the binder were already centered at the greater trochanters, this particular repositioning would not address a documented problem.

choices.label: Increase binder tension at the current position
choices.rationale: Increasing tension does not correct a binder centered across the iliac crests. The stem no longer declares the binder tight, but the anatomical placement remains decisive.
choices.temptation: An incompletely compressed ring may lead to tightening the existing device.
choices.counterfactual: A correctly centered device documented to be inadequately secured would instead require adjustment according to its application instructions.

choices.label: Narrow the binder fold at the current position
choices.rationale: Changing the width while leaving the center at the iliac crests does not correct the documented high placement. No unsupported device-specific fold is taught as a remedy.
choices.temptation: Reducing the fabric width can appear to concentrate compression without moving an injured patient.

nodes.displayName: Choose an objective adjunct when a high-risk limb examination is unreliable

nodes.task: Which assessment plan best addresses Victor's evolving calf findings after the first pressure measurement?

choices.counterfactual: If repeated complete compartment assessment and a reliable examination remained reassuring without an evolving abnormality, invasive extension would have less justification.

choices.temptation: The fracture and an existing measurement site make continuation at the same site familiar.
choices.counterfactual: If concern were localized to the anterior compartment and the remaining compartments had already been assessed, focused trending at that site would be reasonable.

choices.temptation: Palpable pulses and uncertain pain reporting may redirect attention toward occult arterial flow abnormalities.
choices.counterfactual: A new pulse discrepancy or other suspected arterial injury would make arterial imaging relevant to a different vascular question.

nodes.displayName: Address ongoing pelvic hemorrhage after completed arterial embolization
nodes.learningObjective: Address ongoing pelvic hemorrhage after completed arterial embolization
nodes.task: Which hemorrhage-control intervention should the hospital team prioritize at Claire's post-embolization reassessment?
nodes.currentUpdate: Claire remains transfusion dependent after pelvic stabilization and selective embolization. The record documents hypotension before embolization, throughout the procedure and at this reassessment, without an intervening sustained response.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record. Fictional observations.

items.label: Angiographic record
items.value: A pelvic arterial focus was embolized. The final runs at the end of that procedure showed no visible extravasation.

items.label: Ongoing course
items.value: Blood pressure is 78/46 mmHg with continued blood-component transfusion. The correctly positioned binder remains in place.

items.label: Other recorded assessment
items.value: Repeat abdominal ultrasound shows no intraperitoneal free fluid; the examination identifies no external source of ongoing blood loss. No interval pelvic hematoma measurement is documented.

choices.label: Preperitoneal pelvic packing with stabilization
choices.rationale: Packing can address pelvic bleeding not controlled by arterial embolization, but this record does not establish that it uniquely outranks repeat angiography. This is an unkeyed clinician-adjudication candidate, not a scored recommendation.
choices.temptation: Persistent bleeding after embolization raises concern for sources not controlled by the treated artery.
choices.counterfactual: Clinician-confirmed conditions identifying a residual nonarterial pelvic source and favoring immediate packing over repeat arterial evaluation would be needed for a unique packing key.

choices.label: Repeat pelvic angiography with possible embolization
choices.rationale: A negative completion run is time-specific and does not exclude missed or recurrent arterial bleeding. Repeated arterial evaluation remains a credible competitor in persistent hemorrhage.
choices.temptation: Ongoing blood loss despite the first embolization can reflect incomplete or newly apparent arterial control.
choices.counterfactual: New arterial extravasation or a clinician-adjudicated high likelihood of an untreated arterial source would favor repeat angiography.

choices.label: Temporary aortic balloon occlusion before source control
choices.rationale: Balloon occlusion is a proposed temporary bridge rather than definitive control and does not resolve the source uncertainty. Its use has important selection and harm concerns; the candidate must not imply routine benefit.
choices.temptation: Profound ongoing hypotension may prompt a bridge proposal while preparing definitive control.
choices.counterfactual: Only a separately justified specialist bridge decision with definitive control arranged could make balloon occlusion a consideration; current evidence does not make it a default response.

nodes.explanation: No single best answer is assigned. Melissa must adjudicate the exact packing-versus-repeat-angiography boundary before scoring this candidate.
nodes.identityDecision: New scored objective and new concept identity.
reasoningSteps: Interpret persistent transfusion-dependent shock after a time-specific negative completion run without assuming that all arterial bleeding has been excluded.
Compare complementary packing with repeat arterial evaluation; the available evidence does not establish a unique priority in this exact constructed record.

choices.counterfactual: A focal neurologic deficit unexplained after the CT assessment would favor cervical MRI.

review.title: New focal motor change after head injury
clarityIssues: The later examination is identifiable in the exhibit, but 'for Daniel's later neurologic examination' is awkward: the investigation evaluates a change, not an examination.
Intubation and eye responses add GCS detail without making the unchanged best motor response a consequential competing interpretation in the offered options.

cues.why: Together with unchanged ventilator settings, this explicitly disposes of 'Repeat arterial blood-gas analysis'; a nonmedical reader can see that the offered repeat repeats an already reported measurement.
Only this investigation is labelled urgent, giving it a priority-language advantage in a task asking what to prioritize.

fairness: Urgent CT is the defensible best offered investigation for a confirmed new unilateral deficit after head trauma. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The current question does not meaningfully test the proposed best-GCS trap: none of the choices relies on unchanged best motor response, and the repeat gas is already answered.

This is an offline editorial review of all 19 executable candidate nodes using the specified visible fields; key position and author self-assessments were not treated as evidence. No source verification or clinical approval is claimed. The 18 retirement proposals and one unkeyed BCVI gap are not scored; historical held records are only noted. Existing focal-change holds remain unresolved.
suggestions: Ask which investigation should evaluate the new motor change, and balance urgency language across choices.

Replace the already-completed gas foil with a credible competing assessment at this decision stage. If the unchanged best-GCS construct is retained, make that actual decision error compete with escalation while preserving the focal findings.
Keep the later CT result out of this node; the current sequence correctly does so.

review.title: Acute subdural evacuation despite preserved responsiveness
fairness: The reported 12 mm acute subdural thickness supports evacuation despite modest shift and retained command following. Observation and ICP-directed medical treatment are credible errors if the learner overweights those reassuring findings, but are not equally good substitutes here.

Interpret the discordant size, shift and examination, then choose operative rather than observational or pressure-directed management. The named diagnosis is appropriate because the task tests management, not diagnosis.

The right-sided collection coheres with left-arm weakness. This node has enough current examination and CT information to stand alone with its case presentation. Earlier feedback prompts structural reassessment but does not supply the evacuation criterion.
Editorial PASS does not resolve the case's carried holds or confer clinician approval.

review.title: Disposition after negative head CT during apixaban use
clarityIssues: 'There is no additional indication being considered for antithrombotic treatment in this exercise' introduces a medication-treatment issue that none of the choices asks the learner to resolve. It can confuse the existing apixaban indication with the disposition decision.

cues.why: The task partly selects home discharge before comparing it with two admission choices; 'disposition' would be neutral.

cues.phrase: No other injury or medical indication for admission was identified
cues.why: This global admission conclusion risks ruling out both admission options by wording. Necessary observations and home support should remain, but the conclusion should not decide the task.
This is a weak alternative to the genuine routine-repeat-CT misconception; it supplies little resident-level competition in this negative-CT, unchanged-examination scenario.

fairness: The discharge key is defensible for the stated negative CT, baseline examination and reliable home support. The explanation appropriately includes delayed-hemorrhage precautions rather than implying zero risk.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The existing owner hold on this boundary remains unresolved; this review does not adjudicate or remove it.

The normal examination, improving course and support are necessary fairness information, not reasons to remove all reassuring findings. The present construction mostly tests one anticoagulation/disposition rule.
suggestions: Ask which disposition is appropriate and remove the irrelevant sentence about additional antithrombotic indications.

Replace the broad admission-eligibility conclusion with actual findings. Compare plausible disposition strategies and make one supported patient-specific consideration materially affect the routine-admission misconception.
If retained as focused guideline recall, obtain explicit acceptance of that basic educational role instead of calling it a difficult two-step item.

review.title: Correcting pelvic binder position

cues.why: Directly undermines the only tightening alternative while the exhibit emphasizes a different binder level.

cues.phrase: Remove the binder and continue padded transport
cues.why: In an actively transfused pelvic-ring injury this is an obviously less protective plan, leaving the anatomical correction as the only sensible adjustment.

fairness: The described high binder position supports recentering over the greater trochanters. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The hemodynamic trajectory establishes urgency but does not change the keyed landmark correction: the same answer follows without it. This remains a landmark recall item with a clinical wrapper.
suggestions: Either seek explicit acceptance as a brief safety/technique item or redesign around a genuine mechanical-treatment decision in which position and response both change the action.
Use credible temporary-stabilization alternatives and preserve the necessary anatomical observation; do not obscure the location merely to make the question harder.

review.title: Pelvic arterial extravasation despite improved pressure
clarityIssues: Pressure during the scan is supplied, but the immediate post-scan trajectory at the treatment decision is less explicit. The distinction matters if a stronger packing-versus-angiography competitor is introduced.

cues.phrase: Pelvic stabilization with serial hemoglobin testing
cues.why: The sequence has already performed binder correction and still reports ongoing transfusion. This choice largely repeats completed support while only the key offers a new targeted bleeding intervention.

cues.phrase: Definitive pelvic fixation as the next intervention
cues.why: Definitive reconstruction is a weak competitor during continuing hemorrhage resuscitation, so the apparent two-step interpretation has little meaningful competition.

fairness: An enlarging arterial contrast focus and continuing transfusion support angiography/embolization among these options. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The returned data are necessary and the sequence is coherent. The node can stand alone with the supplied injury context; prior binder feedback does not give away embolization.
Although the learner can interpret extravasation and consider the response, the options reduce the scored decision to recognition of active arterial bleeding.
suggestions: Replace definitive fixation with a clinically credible competing hemorrhage-control strategy, then supply the current response and workflow facts needed to distinguish it fairly.
Keep actual perfusion and transfusion observations rather than announcing that angiography is feasible or preferred.

review.title: Persistent neurologic deficit after negative cervical CT

cues.phrase: with multiplanar reconstructions and no motion limitation
cues.why: Directly disposes of 'Repeat cervical CT with reconstructions' by stating that exactly that adequate study is already complete. These adequacy facts are necessary, but the repeat is a spent foil.
A weak next-study alternative during an acute persistent neurologic deficit; the remaining novel study is MRI.

fairness: MRI is the defensible next study for persistent bilateral neurologic findings unexplained by an adequate bony CT. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The observations support cord localization, but the option set permits the simpler rule 'persistent deficit plus negative CT means MRI' without consequential competing interpretation.
suggestions: Retain scan adequacy and the raw neurologic observations; improve the alternatives rather than deleting information needed to establish the CT limitation.
Use a credible competing localization or evaluation pathway that the supplied distribution and course actually distinguish, or accept this explicitly as a basic imaging-safety item.

review.title: Progressive deficit with cervical cord compression
clarityIssues: The explanation contrasts the MRI with a fracture-negative CT that is not restated in this node. The choice is still answerable independently, but the feedback should remain understandable when this later node is selected alone.

cues.why: Makes continued serial examination the already-failing approach; only decompression actively addresses the reported indentation.
Offers recovery care during active neurologic deterioration, an implausibly premature alternative rather than a difficult resident error.

fairness: Worsening deficits with a persistent compressive lesion support early spine-team decompression. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The sequence is clinically coherent and prior MRI feedback does not prescribe decompression. Current findings are sufficient to answer without the preceding node.
The task asks for a definitive plan, while serial observation and rehabilitation are different care stages; this further narrows the choice without substantive reasoning.
suggestions: Use a neutral treatment-plan task and credible competing spine-management strategies at the same decision stage.
If retaining the progressive emergency presentation, label and seek acceptance of a safety-recognition role; do not manufacture ambiguity by hiding the deterioration.
Restate the relevant earlier CT finding in brief if the explanation continues to rely on it in standalone delivery.

review.title: Vascular screening after a transverse-foramen fracture
fairness: The fracture location must be translated into arterial risk despite a normal neurologic examination, then into the appropriate vascular imaging modality. Duplex is a credible modality error and cord MRI a credible wrong-target error.
CTA is the best offered screening study. No confident clinical inaccuracy or missing decision-critical fact identified.

The CTA option names more anatomy than its competitors, but arterial imaging is represented in two choices and the stem does not echo carotid/vertebral labels. This is not a convincing knowledge-free key selector.

review.title: Antithrombotic treatment versus stenting for BCVI
fairness: The learner must interpret the intimal injury and narrowing, then choose treatment while weighing absent bleeding contraindications against absence of an intervention-driving complication. Observation and routine stenting represent consequential errors.
Aspirin is defensible among the offered options. The item does not claim that aspirin is uniquely superior to all other antithrombotic agents; none is offered as a competing key.
The current CTA and bleeding assessment allow standalone answering with the shared presentation. Earlier feedback teaches why to screen but does not supply the treatment choice.

The explanation's 'nonprogressive' is stronger than a single returned CTA establishes, but there is no documented progression requiring intervention. This is a precision issue, not a competing-key defect.
suggestions: For precision, describe the absence of reported progression rather than asserting proven nonprogression from a single study.

review.title: Abnormal ABI in a perfused injured limb
fairness: The resident must reconcile a warm foot and retained function with abnormal pulse/ABI findings, then distinguish imaging from both observation and immediate exploration.

CTA is the best offered assessment in this stable patient without the supplied hard signs. The ABI value is clearly abnormal rather than a borderline measurement that would make repeat measurement equally defensible.

Listing absent hard signs establishes the imaging-versus-operation boundary; these are necessary clinical observations, not nonmedical wording eliminations. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

review.title: Reperfusion and stabilization sequence for an ischemic limb
fairness: The resident must recognize the newly threatened but viable limb and reconcile urgent reperfusion with a grossly unstable skeleton. Temporary shunting bridges these competing priorities.

All choices describe actual operative sequences; fixation first delays perfusion, while definitive repair first risks the reconstruction during subsequent skeletal work. Shunting is the defensible best offered sequence under these facts.
Only the key includes three stages, but its additional step is the tested clinical technique rather than explanatory padding; counting stages alone does not establish correctness.

The update explicitly changes the previously warm foot to a cool pulseless foot, so the sequence is coherent. The current CTA, operative control, skeletal instability and viability findings also support standalone delivery. Earlier feedback does not teach shunting.

review.title: Clinical compartment syndrome with palpable pulses

cues.phrase: Pain rises despite increasing analgesic use
cues.why: Directly marks the analgesia/serial-examination choice as the already-failing plan.
The only urgent treatment competes with continued failed support and another diagnostic delay in an extensively signposted progressive emergency.

fairness: Progressive pain, passive-stretch pain, tense swelling and sensory change after dressing release support immediate fasciotomy; palpable pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

This is an important safety concept, but recognition followed by its standard treatment does not yield two consequential decisions when both alternatives postpone treatment and the examination is so classic.
suggestions: Retain the warning signs and seek explicit safety-recognition acceptance, or redesign the objective around a real assessment-versus-treatment boundary with credible alternatives.

If the task tests the need for pressure confirmation, offer that actual competing plan and make clinical examination reliability explicit; do not weaken emergency findings solely to manufacture difficulty.

review.title: Persistent symptoms after incomplete leg fasciotomy

cues.why: Almost directly matches 'deep posterior compartment release'; the alternative compartments are explicitly described as soft.

cues.phrase: Anterior, lateral and superficial posterior fascia were opened
cues.why: Combined with 'soleus attachment ... was left intact', the operation note names completed sites and advertises the omitted access. Selecting the only remaining compartment can replace anatomical reasoning.

cues.phrase: Complete the deep posterior compartment release
cues.why: 'Complete' agrees with the narrated omission, whereas the other release repeats already soft, opened compartments.

fairness: Completing an unreleased deep posterior compartment is the defensible answer to the supplied operative record and persistent findings. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The sequence coheres with the preceding fasciotomy decision and contains enough postoperative detail to stand alone. Earlier feedback does not reveal the missing compartment, but this node's own wording does.
Potentially valuable applied surgical anatomy has been reduced to a named-omission and location-matching task.
suggestions: Retain technically accurate operative observations but require interpretation of access and residual muscle/sensory findings rather than repeating the keyed compartment's name in the examination.
Compare plausible corrections at the same operative stage, with clinician-checked anatomy that distinguishes them. Avoid solving the cue merely by replacing anatomical terms with awkward synonyms.

review.title: Compartment assessment when sedation limits examination
clarityIssues: 'Repeat arterial duplex ultrasound' implies an earlier duplex that the visible record never describes.

cues.why: Names the capability used by 'Serial intracompartmental pressure measurement' and no other option. This is a direct answer-specific availability cue.
Together with the singled-out pressure capability, this rehearses the exact monitoring plan subsequently explained as correct.

fairness: Pressure measurement as an adjunct to serial examinations is defensible in this sedated high-risk patient. The explanation correctly describes supplementation, not a universal isolated pressure cutoff.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The civilian setting can remain if needed to define the intended clinical context; explicitly naming the keyed capability is unnecessary with these alternatives.
After the capability sentence, little remains beyond matching an unreliable examination to the named monitoring tool.
suggestions: Remove the answer-specific capability statement while retaining the setting and ability to perform ongoing observation in neutral terms.
Change 'Repeat' to an initial duplex unless a prior study and its limitations are actually supplied.
Make examination reliability and the evolving findings distinguish credible diagnostic strategies; do not add unsupported pressure thresholds.

review.title: Persistent pelvic hemorrhage after embolization
clarityIssues: 'Pressure again falls' leaves unclear whether shock persisted continuously through embolization or recurred after a durable response; that chronology affects repeat angiography versus packing.
The record does not state how interval pelvic hematoma enlargement was established at the reassessment.

cues.phrase: Completion runs show no further arterial extravasation
cues.why: Risks making repeat angiography a completed-test foil if read as proof that arterial bleeding can no longer occur, although clinically it is only a time-specific result.

cues.phrase: Definitive internal fixation of the pelvic ring
cues.why: An implausibly definitive reconstruction during recurrent shock; it does not provide a strong third hemorrhage-control competitor.

fairness: Packing is plausible for ongoing nonarterial pelvic hemorrhage after embolization, and inferring the residual source before choosing complementary control is a useful two-step objective.

Uniqueness is not secure: negative completion runs do not exclude a missed, recurrent or newly apparent arterial source during subsequent hypotension. Repeat angiography can remain defensible. This is a clinician-adjudication uncertainty, not a claim that packing is wrong.

The explanation moves from 'can arise' from other sources to a preferred intervention without sufficiently resolving the competing arterial explanation. A negative repeat abdominal ultrasound is helpful but not absolute exclusion of every other bleeding source.
The moderate rating describes the intended source-and-sequence reasoning; unresolved ambiguity should not be counted as hard difficulty.
suggestions: Have Melissa adjudicate the closest alternative and the exact clinical conditions favoring packing over repeat angiography.

Specify the temporal response to embolization, objective ongoing hemorrhage findings and any genuinely decision-critical logistical constraints using supported facts. Do not invent a cutoff or simply label the bleeding venous.
Replace definitive fixation with a credible hemorrhage-control alternative once the intended decision boundary is established.

review.title: Incomplete cervical CT before collar clearance

cues.phrase: The scan was stopped before the lower cervical levels were acquired
cues.why: Directly supplies the missing-work instruction answered by 'complete cervical CT'; the report repeats the same omission.
The named modality in the presentation further favors completing CT over MRI before the learner has to interpret the clinical context.

fairness: Completing the unacquired anatomy while maintaining the collar is defensible. Unlike an absent export, the acquisition log explicitly proves the anatomy was not scanned; this is a sound fairness distinction.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. However, the duplicated omission plus the named pathway makes this a straightforward completeness check, not two consequential steps.
The shared presentation is needed to identify the hospital's clearance approach. No later completed study should be shown before this decision.
suggestions: Keep one clear acquisition record; remove the redundant restatement of the same missing levels.

Either accept a basic acquisition-safety role or require a meaningful comparison between evidence adequacy and another supported patient consideration. Do not conceal the fact of nonacquisition to force uncertainty.
Review the first explanation together with the second task because it teaches the later CT-clearance rule.

review.title: Collar removal after adequate negative CT in an obtunded adult

cues.why: The presentation names a 'CT-based clearance pathway', and only the key repeats 'under the CT-based pathway'. This is a direct task/presentation/option wording match.

cues.phrase: The unacquired lower levels prevent use of the high-quality CT clearance pathway
cues.why: The preceding node's explanation teaches the exact missing condition; this node supplies it and asks for the rehearsed consequence.

The quality conclusion plus a second complete-source-review row largely certifies eligibility in advance. Actual acquisition observations are useful; repeated eligibility reassurance adds little inference.

fairness: Collar removal is defensible under the explicitly adopted conditional pathway with the supplied negative adequate CT and no focal discrepancy. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The case is coherent and the current findings stand alone when the shared presentation accompanies it. Without that presentation, the reference to the adopted pathway is incomplete.

After the first explanation, this is protocol recall rather than independent two-step reasoning. The named pathway legitimately limits clinical ambiguity, but its wording need not appear only in the keyed option.
suggestions: Place the adopted pathway in shared context and use parallel plain collar plans without repeating its name only in the key.
Avoid certifying eligibility twice; retain the raw adequacy findings needed for fair application.
Redesign the second node around a distinct consequential discrepancy, or explicitly treat it as scaffolded reinforcement rather than a difficult independent scored objective.

review.title: Expanding hematoma despite preserved distal pulses
fairness: The resident must recognize expansion beyond marked borders with recurrent bleeding as a hard vascular sign, then choose exploration despite stable systemic pressure and palpable distal pulses.

CTA is a credible competing sequencing error in a stable patient. The single track and lack of associated skeletal injury narrow the localization problem that might otherwise favor preoperative imaging.
Operative exploration is the defensible best answer for this isolated penetrating-injury scenario. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.
The progression is reported as observations rather than the diagnosis label 'expanding hematoma'; the explanation appropriately supplies that label after answering.

review.title: Disposition after normal penetrating-limb vascular assessment

cues.phrase: The wound has been cleaned and closed
cues.why: Together with an entirely normal completed assessment, this gives the narrative a discharge-ready ending before the disposition decision.

cues.phrase: Discharge with vascular precautions and scheduled follow-up
cues.why: The key is the longest and only explicitly safety-complete follow-up plan; 'CTA before discharge' omits the same routine discharge safeguards, creating an avoidable completeness advantage.

fairness: The reliable normal examination, normal ABI and lack of an associated admission indication support discharge with follow-up. No confident clinical inaccuracy identified.

The normal examination and ABI are necessary to the disposition rule; they should not be removed to manufacture ambiguity. As written, all findings align and no meaningful competing patient consideration requires a second inference.
This is a useful high-yield counterpart to the abnormal-ABI case, but repetition of the opposite side of one rule does not itself establish resident-level difficulty.
suggestions: Put routine wound care, precautions and follow-up in common context and compare parallel decisions about imaging, admission or discharge.

Introduce a supported, clinically meaningful competing consideration only if it changes interpretation of otherwise reassuring testing; otherwise seek explicit acceptance as focused basic vascular-triage practice.

nodes.task: Which investigation should the hospital team prioritize for Daniel's later neurologic examination?
nodes.currentUpdate: Daniel was intubated after an initially unresponsive assessment. Circulation is now stable and there is no ongoing extracranial hemorrhage.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record. Fictional observations.

items.label: Serial examination

nodes.displayName: Use reliable vascular findings and ABI to decide imaging versus follow-up
nodes.learningObjective: Use reliable vascular findings and ABI to decide imaging versus follow-up
nodes.task: Which vascular plan best fits Jasmine's completed hospital assessment?
nodes.currentUpdate: The wound has been cleaned and closed. Jasmine is alert and can cooperate with examination.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record. Fictional observations.

items.label: Examination
items.value: Pedal pulses are symmetric. Motor and sensation are normal. There is no expanding mass, bruit, active bleeding or recorded episode of arterial bleeding.

items.label: Pressures and associated injury
items.value: Injured-leg ABI is 1.04. The opposite ABI is 1.02. Radiographs show no fracture, and there is no other injury requiring admission.

choices.label: Discharge with vascular precautions and scheduled follow-up
choices.rationale: The reliable normal examination and normal ABI support discharge without routine vascular imaging after this isolated penetrating wound. Follow-up remains important for delayed manifestations.
choices.temptation: Applies the same triage rule to genuinely reassuring findings.
choices.counterfactual: A normal reliable assessment supports this follow-up plan.

choices.label: CTA before discharge
choices.rationale: CTA is useful for abnormal indices or examination findings. Wound proximity alone does not require routine CTA after the represented reassuring assessment.
choices.temptation: Images every penetrating wound near an arterial course.
choices.counterfactual: An ABI below 0.9 or abnormal vascular findings would support CTA.

choices.label: Inpatient vascular observation with repeat ABI
choices.rationale: Admission can fit an unreliable examination or another injury. Those circumstances are absent here.
choices.temptation: Assumes repeated inpatient testing is required despite a completed reliable assessment.
choices.counterfactual: An unreliable examination or associated admission need would make continued hospital assessment reasonable.

nodes.deletionTest: Reliability, mechanism and associated-injury details are eligibility boundaries. Removing them makes discharge less defensible. The opposite ABI corroborates measurement context without introducing a new cutoff.

claims.statement: A component prevented by an airway tube should be marked not testable with its interference recorded, without manufacturing a numeric total.
claims.limitation: One guideline lineage supports this point. Independent corroboration remains a review limitation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Separately recorded motor responses convey changes that a global summary score can conceal.
claims.limitation: One guideline lineage supports this point. Independent corroboration remains a review limitation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Early severe TBI with polytrauma requires urgent neurologic examination and cranial CT after life-threatening hemorrhage control.
claims.limitation: Consensus addresses early severe TBI with polytrauma. Applying its priority to a new unilateral deficit is clinical synthesis requiring review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Acute traumatic subdural hematoma thicker than 10 mm or producing more than 5 mm midline shift meets the surgical-evacuation criterion regardless of GCS.
claims.limitation: Older nonrandomized evidence. The constructed 12 mm measurement crosses the thickness criterion.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: A life-threatening traumatic brain mass lesion warrants urgent neurosurgical intervention after systemic bleeding control.
claims.limitation: One guideline lineage supports this point. Independent corroboration remains a review limitation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Routine mild-head-injury decision rules should not exclude CT in adults taking an anticoagulant.
claims.limitation: One guideline lineage supports this point. Independent corroboration remains a review limitation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Routine repeat head imaging is unnecessary after a CT without hemorrhage in a neurologically baseline anticoagulated adult.
claims.limitation: New symptoms or neurologic deterioration require a new assessment. CDC implements ACEP 2023 and supplies one evidence lineage.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Anticoagulant use does not itself require admission after negative head CT when the examination is baseline and other admission indications are absent.
claims.limitation: Owner decision review.n3.head-injury-rule-scope-and-anticoagulant-exposure.v2 remains active. No anticoagulant resumption or withholding regimen is inferred.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Mild-head-injury discharge counseling includes delayed-hemorrhage warning symptoms and follow-up instructions.
claims.limitation: One guideline lineage supports this point. Independent corroboration remains a review limitation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Temporary circumferential pelvic stabilization centers compression at the greater-trochanter level.
claims.limitation: One guideline lineage supports this point. Independent corroboration remains a review limitation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Circumferential pelvic compression provides temporary early stabilization during hemorrhage resuscitation.
claims.limitation: One guideline lineage supports this point. Independent corroboration remains a review limitation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Pelvic arterial contrast extravasation can justify angiography and embolization after blood pressure improves.
claims.limitation: This concerns a resuscitated patient with an arterial target and supplies no universal sequence for uncontrolled shock.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Persistent pelvic hemorrhage with hemodynamic instability after angiography supports preperitoneal packing with pelvic stabilization.
claims.limitation: Packing and angiography are complementary. Source reassessment and center resources matter.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Neurologic findings after cervical trauma can require MRI despite CT showing no fracture or malalignment.
claims.limitation: One specialist recommendation set. CT-negative clearance does not apply to a new neurologic discrepancy.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Progressive neurologic loss with continuing cervical cord compression supports early surgical decompression.
claims.limitation: No universal surgical-hour cutoff, steroid regimen or perfusion target is prescribed.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: A cervical fracture extending into a transverse foramen is a high-risk pattern warranting CTA screening for blunt cerebrovascular injury.
claims.limitation: Evidence quality and population scope require clinical review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Confirmed blunt cerebrovascular injury generally warrants antithrombotic treatment when bleeding risk permits.
claims.limitation: Several agents are reasonable. No aspirin-versus-heparin superiority or dose is inferred.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Routine stenting of grade II or III blunt cerebrovascular injury adds no established benefit to antithrombotic treatment.
claims.limitation: Selected progressive or symptomatic lesions can require intervention.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Repeat CTA near seven days can refute a provisional BCVI diagnosis and support treatment cessation when the initial finding was spasm or misinterpretation.
claims.limitation: Conditional low-quality evidence. Adequate repeat imaging and original-image review are necessary. Healing of a confirmed lesion is a different scenario.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Stable penetrating lower-extremity injury with abnormal vascular examination or ABI below 0.9 warrants vascular imaging.
claims.limitation: Evidence quality and population scope require clinical review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: CTA is an appropriate primary vascular study when stable penetrating limb trauma requires imaging.
claims.limitation: Evidence quality and population scope require clinical review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: An expanding hematoma supports operative exploration for arterial injury in an isolated penetrating limb wound.
claims.limitation: Associated skeletal or shotgun injuries can require localization imaging. The draft has neither.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: A reliable normal vascular examination and ABI greater than 0.9 can support discharge after isolated penetrating lower-limb trauma with follow-up.
claims.limitation: This excludes knee dislocation, high-energy blunt injury, unreliable examination and other admission needs.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: An inadequately perfused limb needing fracture stabilization can receive a temporary vascular shunt before fixation and definitive vascular reconstruction.
claims.limitation: Low-quality evidence. Sequence depends on perfusion and injury. No fixed safe ischemia duration is taught.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Palpable distal pulses do not exclude dangerous compartment-related tissue ischemia.
claims.limitation: Evidence quality and population scope require clinical review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Increasing analgesic requirement, painful passive stretch and progressive tense swelling support acute compartment syndrome after limb injury.
claims.limitation: Evidence quality and population scope require clinical review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Established acute leg compartment syndrome requires prompt complete compartment release.
claims.limitation: Military guidance supports completeness anatomy. Civilian drafts exclude late irreversible ischemia and prophylaxis thresholds.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Complete leg fasciotomy includes the deep posterior compartment, accessed by separating soleus attachment from the posterior tibia.
claims.limitation: Shared operative anatomy. Protected figures and procedural prose are excluded.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: For a high-risk civilian patient unable to report symptoms reliably, compartment pressure measurement can supplement repeated clinical assessment.
claims.limitation: JTS discourages routine measurements in the deployed environment. This is a monitored civilian hospital case. A single pressure is not a universal diagnosis.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: CT-based cervical clearance requires adequate high-quality imaging with coverage of the cervical spine.
claims.limitation: Applying the high-quality CT criterion to a documented incomplete acquisition is explicit synthesis. Repeat versus retrieval depends on actual acquisition coverage.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: Under the EAST conditional protocol, a negative high-quality cervical CT can support collar removal in an obtunded adult blunt-trauma patient.
claims.limitation: Conditional very-low-quality evidence. The draft supplies protocol adoption and excludes a focal discrepancy.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with the stated traumatic injury in an outside-hospital record

claims.statement: MRI can depict selected traumatic axonal injuries that conventional CT may underdetect.
claims.limitation: This supports the modality distinction. The exact priority of repeat CT versus MRI for the constructed new focal change remains a carried clinical/source-review question.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with traumatic brain injury
